3. On 26.10.92 the writ petitioner sent a Memo to respondent No. 2 stating that he was on leave and was not connected with the offence and requested a cancellation of the impugned order, with no effect. It is the case of the writ petitioner that respondent No. 5, Mr. Abdul Matin, who is a member of Parliament from Chandpur 256 Constituency, Hajiganj is his political rival and it is at his behest and instigation that he was entangled in a false criminal case and suspended. The writ petitioner obtained an ad-interim bail on 7.2.93 from the High Court Division in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 252 of 1993 in the criminal case in question, namely, Hajiganj PS Case No. 3 dated 16.9.92 and ever since 7.2.93 he is not under any disability to run the affairs of the Union Parishad. Soon after he obtained the ad-interim bail on 7.2.93 an order of detention by Memo No. 85 dated 24.2.93 was passed against him under the signature of respondent No. 3, the Deputy Commissioner, Chandpur detaining him for a period of 30 days under section 3(2) of the Special Powers Act, 1974. The order of detention was amended by respondent No. 3 on 3.3.93 making the order of detention effective from the date of his arrest. The writ petitioner challenged the legality of the order of detention in Writ Petition No. 406 of 1993 whereupon a Division Bench of the High Court Division issued a Rule Nisi upon the respondents on 28.3.93 and stayed the operation of the impugned order dated 3.3.93 for 8 weeks from date. The writ petitioner asserted that he was neither absconding nor had he been taken into custody and after obtaining an ad-interim bail on 7.2.93 he was obstructed mala fide from resuming the functions of the Union Parishad by the issuance of the order of detention, but now he has been functioning as Chairman of the said Union Parishad. 

 4. The affidavit-in-opposition of the Government-appellant was cryptic. It merely stated that after the lodging of the FIR in Hajiganj PS Case No. 3 dated 16.3.92 the Superintendent of Police, Chandpur, sought permission from the Deputy Commissioner, Chandpur to arrest the writ petitioner. The Deputy Commissioner, Chandpur by a Memo dated 7.10.92 informed the matter to the concerned Ministry which then issued the order of suspension. It was denied that the writ petitioner was running the affairs of the Union Parishad. It was stated that Mr. Md. Siddiqur Rahman Khan, an elected Member of the Union Parishad, was elected as the Acting Chairman who is running the affairs of the Union Parishad. As the criminal proceedings have not yet been terminated the order of suspension will remain. 

 5. The affidavit-in-opposition and the supplementary affidavit in-opposition of respondent No. 5 are however more detailed and contain more information than that of the Government-appellant. Besides denying his personal involvement in the criminal case and in the order of suspension, respondent No. 5 narrated in details the involvement of the writ petitioner in several criminal proceedings since 1972 including the present Hajiganj PS Case No. 3 dated 16.10.92, as also his other conducts. Respondent No. 5 also annexed in his supplementary affidavit two Annexures, Annexure-3 and Annexure-4 to which we shall revert in due course. 

 6. The learned Judges of the High Court Division in a lengthy judgment unnecessarily took note of the elaborate submissions made by the learned Advocates of both sides, but lost track of the submissions in course of giving its own findings which were confined to only a few pages. Relying on the case of Abdul Hye Bhuiyan Vs. Secretary, Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development and Co-operatives, 1981 BLD (AD) 196, the learned Judges held that the impugned order does not reveal any application of mind of the Government, because the action was taken solely on the ground of pendency of a criminal case against the writ petitioner but the impugned order does not reveal what relationship the criminal proceeding has with the exercise of power by him as Chairman of the Union Parishad and how the criminal proceeding is likely to be prejudicial to the interest of the Union Parishad or undesirable from the point of view of public interest. As already noticed the Rule Nisi was made absolute. 

 "65. Suspension of Chairman and members in certain circumstances—(1) Where any proceedings have been initiated for the removal of the Chairman under section 12 or where any criminal proceedings under any law have been started against such Chairman or where on an enquiry by the Government, he is found to be guilty of any misconduct within the meaning of section 12(1) and in the opinion of the Government, the exercise of power by him as Chairman is either likely to be prejudicial to the interest of the Union Parishad or undersirable from the point of view of public interest, the Government may, by order in writing, place such Chairman under suspension, and during the period of suspension, an Acting Chairman elected in accordance with the provisions of section 16 shall discharge the functions of the Chairman until the termination of the proceedings or, in the event of the Chairman being removed as a result of such proceedings, or until the suspension is withdrawn or until a new Chairman is elected for the Union Parishad. (2)………………………………………………” 

 9. Three alternative circumstances provide the occasion for the government to exercise the power of suspension of Chairman:—(1) where any proceedings have been initiated for the removal of the Chairman under section 12; or (2) where any criminal proceedings under any law have been started against such Chairman; or (3) where on an enquiry by the Government, he is found to be guilty of any misconduct within the meaning of section 12(1). But these circumstances provide only the basis or the foundation for the exercise of power of suspension. It is further conditional upon a formation of opinion by the Government that the exercise of power by the person concerned as Chairman is either likely to be prejudicial to the interest of the Union Parishad or undesirable from the point of view of public interest. 

 10. Whenever in any statute the exercise of power by any authority is made conditional upon the formation of opinion of such authority, the formation of opinion is a sine qua non for the exercise of such power. Mere existence of any of the three circumstances mentioned in section 65(1) will not be enough. The Government also must form an opinion in terms of the language mentioned in section 65(1). The opinion is formed by the Government after considering the materials before it and after being satisfied that the materials have a causal connection with the kind of opinion that it is required to form. If there are no materials at all on which to form an opinion or if the materials that exist are totally unconnected with the kind of opinion that the Government is required to form, then the order of suspension will fall through. There is to be some indication in the order of suspension itself that the criminal proceedings started against the Chairman is either likely to be prejudicial to the interest of Union Parishad or undesirable from the point of view of public interest, but it is not necessary that the entire materials on which the opinion has been formed should be disclosed in the impugned order itself, although, if challenged on the ground of absence of materials or non-application of mind, the Government will be obliged to place the materials before the Court to show whether it acted on materials on record and/or applied its mind. The co-relationship of criminal proceedings with the kind of opinion required to be formed under section 65(1) will be a matter of deduction from existing materials which will vary from case to case and which cannot be reduced to a precise formula. The gravity of the offence disclosed in the criminal proceedings may be a sweeping factor in the minds of the people of the locality and a public murmur about a Chairman's involvement in a capital crime may also be a burning issue among the members of the public but if the issues of gravity and public murmur are not before Government as materials for formation of opinion then these are extraneous matters and cannot be taken into consideration by the Court itself when the order of suspension is scrutinised by the Court. It is for the Government to form its opinion and the Court will not substitute its own opinion for the opinion of the Government. The Court will only see that there were materials before the Government for forming an opinion. and that there is a causal connection between the materials and the opinion. Even the sufficiency of the material is not for the Court to consider. 

 Reading the impugned order as a whole, which we have quoted in full, it is clear that the Government did not take a grave view of the fact that the Chairman was implicated in a capital crime or that the exercise of power by him as Chairman with such a stigma attached and with a popular feeling running against him is either likely to be prejudicial to the interest of the Union Parishad or undesirable from the point of view of public interest. There are also no materials to that effect. What carried the Government was not the pendency of a criminal proceeding as such, and held by the High Court Division, but its reliance upon the fact, based on materials, that for fear of arrest by the police the writ petitioner remained absconding from the date of occurrence of the alleged murder as a result of which the day to day and developmental activities of the Union Parishad were being hampered. It is the Government's reliance upon the fact of his abscondence to avoid arrest in the criminal proceeding that weighed heavily with the Government in forming an opinion in the matter. The High Court Division completely failed to consider that this is not a case where there was no formation of opinion at all. The impugned order clearly shows that an opinion was formed and was expressed, definitely and decisively. Considerable materials were there before the Government for formation of opinion in the way it has been formed. Seven out of nine members of the Union Parishad addressed a letter dated 27.9.92 to the Thana Nirbahi Officer, Hajiganj stating that in the meeting dated 16.9.92 there was no resolution regarding any leave of absence to be granted to the writ petitioner and no such resolution was ever moved or passed. (Annexure-3 to the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition of respondent No. 5) The Deputy Commissioner, Chandpur by a Memo. dated 7.10.92 wrote to the Ministry concerned stating the facts of the Hajiganj PS case No. 3 dated 16.9.92 and stating also that he gave approval of arrest of the writ petitioner as prayed for by the Superintendent of Police, Chandpur, but as the writ petitioner was absconding from the date of occurrence he could not as yet be arrested. The Deputy Commissioner also stated about a Memo of the Thana Nirbani Officer dated 29.9.92 pointing out that in the absence of the Chairman the day to day activities of the Union Parishad are being hampered. The Deputy Commissioner also stated that the absconding Chairman wrote a letter to him asking for approval of leave of absence for 3 months on the ground of illness but he neither mentioned any specific disease nor enclosed any medical certificate. The Deputy Commissioner also mentioned about the Memo dated 3.10.92 written by the Thana Nirbahi Officer to him enclosing therewith the application of 7 members of the Union Parishad dated 27.9.92 stating that there was no resolution granting leave of absence to the Chairman on 16.9.92. He further stated that the writ petitioner filed his application for approval of leave only to avoid arrest. The writ petitioner did not even enclose a copy of the alleged resolution dated 16.9.92. The Deputy Commissioner then sought for necessary directions from the Government regarding the absconding Chairman. This Memo of the Deputy Commissioner is Annexure 4 to the Supplementary affidavit-in-opposition of respondent No. 5. The order of suspension followed. 

 11. It was incumbent upon the High Court Division under such circumstances, before making the Rule Nisi absolute, to come to a finding that there were materials before the Government to form an opinion that the writ petitioner's plea of leave of absence for 3 months was true and the Deputy Commissioner's letter to the Government alleging his abscondence was wrong. No such finding was given. We for ourselves do not find any reason to disbelieve, for the purpose of section 65(1) of the Ordinance, Annexures 3 and 4 to the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition of respondent No.5 which are official documents. The writ petitioner was clearly found to be an absconder and his story of leave of absence for 3 months was disbelieved by the Government on available materials. If on the institution of a criminal proceeding against a Chairman, he absconds himself to avoid arrest and the activities of the Union Parishad suffer thereby the fact of his abscondence occasioned by a criminal proceeding inevitably connects the criminal proceeding with the kind of opinion required to be formed under section 65(1) and it cannot be said that under the circumstances the Government failed to apply its mind or that materials do not exist for formation of opinion or that the impugned order of suspension does not reveal any co-relationship between the criminal proceeding and the opinion. In the criminal proceeding however, the criminal Court will come to an independent decision on the basis of the evidence on record in the criminal case itself, as to whether the writ petitioner absconded or not, if such a fact is alleged. 

 "16. Acting Chairman—(1) If a vacancy occurs in the office of Chairman or if the Chairman is unable to discharge the functions of his office on account of absence, illness or any other cause, a member elected by the Union Parishad from amongst the elected members shall act as Acting Chairman until a new Chairman elected to fill such vacancy enters upon his office or until the Chairman resumes the functions of his, office, as the case may be. (2)……………………………………………………….. 

 16. We cannot give any other meaning to the word 'absence' than the one referred to in section 15. To 'abscond' in its dictionary meaning means departing secretly fleeing from the law. To equate abscondence with absence is to do violence to the word "absence" which in its dictionary meaning means being away from a place or person. Fleeing from the law and being away are not the same thing. Nor can we bring abscondence within "any other cause". The words "any other cause" have to be read ejusdem generis with the words "absence, illness". It must be a cause of a like nature. The application of section 65(1) of the Ordinance in the facts and circumstances of the case was well-justified and the impugned order of suspension does not suffer from any legal infirmity. 

 17. It was argued before the High Court Division that the impugned order was illegal because it was not preceded by a show cause notice to the writ petitioner. The High Court Division noted the argument in great details but failed to give any decision in the matter, without telling why. While granting leave we left this question to be agitated afresh by the writ petitioner-respondent and Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed has argued the matter in details. The learned Additional Attorney-General points out that at least in this case the plea of absence of a show cause notice is not available, because the writ petitioner was absconding. We find the submission of the learned Additional Attorney-General to be quite reasonable in the facts and circumstances of the case. 

 18. From what we have discussed and held above we would have allowed the appeal, but our decision is otherwise for the following reason. We find that neither the Government had any materials before it nor did it ever consider that the writ petitioner being involved in a capital crime there was a public murmur against him or that his very involvement in a capital crime raised a question mark as to his suitability or desirability to continue with a public representative office. The Government was swayed by the fact of his abscondence after the occurrence. We do not know what would have been the opinion of the Government had there been a mere pendency of the aforesaid criminal proceedings and no abscondence by the writ petitioner. It cannot be said from the impugned order itself and from the materials furnished that the Government formed an opinion to suspend the writ petitioner anyway even if he was not absconding. In that view of the matter we think that the impugned order of suspension cannot continue when the abscondence comes to an end and on being granted bail the writ petitioner is ready and willing to perform the functions of Chairman. He obtained bail on 7.2.93 and although an order of detention was passed against him on 24.2.92 with further amendment on 3.3.93 he obtained a stay thereof in Writ Petition No.406 of 1993 on 28.3.93. The Office of Chairman is a public representative office and its deprivation, however temporary, will be strictly viewed at. The writ petitioner being now available for running the affairs of the Union Parishad as Chairman and the Government's very basis of formation of opinion being non-existent, at least now the order of suspension cannot be allowed to operate any more than it was necessary. It is on record that a charge-sheet under sections 147/148/149/323/324/ 325/379/302 of the Penal Code in the said Hajiganj PS Case No. 3 of 16.9.92 has been submitted against the writ petitioner and 13 others on 15.11.92 and Mr. TH Khan submits that in the event the illegality of the impugned order of suspension is upheld, the Government should be free to take such further steps in the light of developing situations as it may be advised. We need not speculate about the further steps to be taken or not to be taken by the Government. But we have decided not to interfere with the judgment and order of the High Court Division not because the reasonings given by the learned Judges were correct but because the basis on which the Government based its action no longer exists.
